problem: Jalisco's tequila industry leaves behind about 915,000 tonnes of agave bagasse a year, the fibrous residue left after the sugars are extracted (Warren-Vega et al., 2025); the 2.18 million tonnes of agave processed in 2025, reported by the Cámara Nacional de la Industria Tequilera, are consistent with that figure, since roughly 40 percent of the plant's weight ends up as bagasse. Most of it is burned, dumped on roadsides or left in open piles to rot. Distilleries treat it as a cost: the general coordinator of a distillery I interviewed pays 200 to 500 pesos per tonne to have it hauled to composting ramps. Burning releases carbon dioxide and particulates into rural communities; open decomposition releases methane and leachates, and the piles shelter flies, pests and rodents. Meanwhile, a restaurant supplier in my network reports that gourmet species such as shiitake and lion's mane often have to come from other states, or are even imported. The fibre is lignocellulose, exactly what wood-decay fungi eat, so the waste and the food that could come from it sit a few kilometres apart. The same pattern repeats across Latin America with sugarcane bagasse, coffee residues and corn stover.
solution: Fungi Mati grows gourmet mushrooms on pelletized agave bagasse, hydrated, pasteurized and supplemented with 20 percent soybean hull, then inoculated with Pleurotus ostreatus, P. ostreatus var. columbinus or pink oyster (P. djamor), with lion's mane next. In four to six weeks the fungus turns the fibre into food, and the spent substrate goes back to the soil as compost. The home farm in Zapopan is being set up with low-cost equipment bought in September and October 2026: a 39-litre pressure canner as autoclave, a laminar flow hood, and a fruiting room under negative pressure with filtered intake, an inline extractor and humidistat-controlled ultrasonic humidification. Two things make it more than a farm. First, an approved breeding project at the Carrillo Biorefinery Lab of Tec de Monterrey, led by Dr. Danay Carrillo Nieves, where I run the strain collection: controlled crosses between single-spore monokaryons of two parental Pleurotus strains, to obtain a strain better adapted to bagasse. Second, an AI tutor I built on ChatGPT, with guidance and early support from Equitech Futures, delivered through Google Slides and tested in a 50-student course against a traditionally taught control group; the next version will be a chatbot built on Claude.
serve: Three groups. Distilleries and agave growers, who pay to dispose of bagasse or burn it. In 2026 I contacted about 35 people and organizations and held six interviews: a distillery general coordinator who pays 200 to 500 pesos per tonne for hauling, a compost operator who processes a whole distillery's bagasse, the pellet manager who is now my substrate supplier, a neighbour living a kilometre from a distillery, and two bagasse researchers. Field growers and jimadores did not answer, so I start with distilleries, whose residue already costs them money. Restaurants and households in Guadalajara and nearby areas that want fresh gourmet mushrooms grown locally, reached through a restaurant distributor and a well-connected saleswoman in my network, and through a 700-member gourmet food community, many of them foreigners willing to pay for local product. And people who want to learn to grow: my 2026 PrepaTec pilot reached 85 people (50 students, 10 teachers, 5 staff, 20 visitors), I helped teach a two-session course for 50 young women in January, and I sell grow kits and paid courses. For distilleries, a disposal cost becomes a supply chain; for neighbours, less burning and fewer rotting piles.
stage: Pilot, because the solution is running with real users in one community while I still iterate on its design. Between May and June 2026, with a Ruta Azul: Campus Vivo grant from Tec de Monterrey, I turned an abandoned space at PrepaTec Guadalajara into a permanent oyster mushroom farm, taught 50 students to grow there, and from 13 June harvested two abundant flushes that went back to that school community: 85 people in total. That pilot ran on sawdust pellets (about 60 percent biological efficiency). Agave bagasse is the iteration I am testing now: in triplicate bags of unsupplemented bagasse pellets, P. ostreatus var. columbinus gave about 50 percent biological efficiency over the first two weighed flushes, and a third, unweighed flush followed; supplementation with soybean hull is the next test. In October 2026 my pellet supplier began producing a mushroom-specific pellet mix for me. Fungi Mati also sells grow kits and courses, including two paid courses for foreigners in 2026. What is not yet steady is fresh-mushroom supply: the Zapopan home farm, funded by a 5,000 US dollar Equitech Futures award, received its equipment in September and October 2026 and is being set up now.
positioned: I have grown mushrooms since I was ten, and I built Fungi Mati with the people who generate the bagasse and the people who would eat or grow the result. In 2026 I contacted about 35 people and organizations across six channels and held six interviews, which changed the project. The general coordinator of a distillery told me they pay 200 to 500 pesos per tonne to haul bagasse to composting ramps, so my first partner became the distillery, not the field grower, who never answered. A compost operator who processes a whole distillery's bagasse showed that valorization can pay, and named the real barrier: no authorized disposal sites and weak inspection. A pellet manager showed me the collection-and-drying chain already exists; he is now my substrate supplier, and in October he began producing a pellet mix designed for mushrooms. A woman living a kilometre from a distillery said the smell and flies no longer bother her because they are used to them, so I frame the social value as preventing a documented harm, not answering a demand. In an August meeting, Dr. Ramón Rodríguez Macías of the Universidad de Guadalajara, whose doctorate is on agave bagasse, pushed me to treat it as a by-product and to measure public-health impact. On the demand side, 85 people took part in the PrepaTec pilot, 50 young women took a course I helped teach, and paying course customers and kit buyers told me what they need to grow at home. I run the fungal strain collection at the Carrillo Biorefinery Lab of Tec de Monterrey, under Dr. Danay Carrillo Nieves. I lead B-Eco, a student environmental group of 20 volunteers, and I am a beVisioneers fellow with venture coaching. I am from Zapopan, in the state that produces the bagasse.
innovative: Most mushroom farms in Mexico grow on whatever straw is at hand, from wheat to corn stover, or on sawdust pellets, and treat the substrate as a commodity. Fungi Mati starts from the opposite end: the region's most abundant residue, agave bagasse, which today is burned, dumped or composted slowly, and turns it into gourmet mushrooms in four to six weeks. That speed is the core of the solution. In the time it takes compost to half-break down, the same fibre has already become a food that sells by the kilogram, and the spent substrate still returns to the soil as compost. Pelletized bagasse makes this repeatable: pellets standardize moisture and particle size, store for months without spoiling, and cost about half of a conventional substrate at the local price of 22,000 to 24,000 pesos per tonne, so a small grower can prepare substrate the same way every time. Of the ten existing bagasse uses I benchmarked, from adobe bricks and briquettes to bioplastics and compost, none turns it into a high-value food through a low-cost model a small producer can run. The system needs no industrial plant, which makes it replicable at the scale of a town near a distillery, and knowledge ships with the product through an AI tutor, built with guidance and early support from Equitech Futures and tested against traditional teaching in a 50-student course. As an exploratory line, at the Carrillo Biorefinery Lab, with Dr. Danay Carrillo Nieves, I will test whether crossing single-spore monokaryons of two Pleurotus parental strains yields a strain better adapted to bagasse; if it does, the method travels to spent coffee grounds, corn stover or sugarcane bagasse. The broader idea is a method for matching residues with fungi, starting with the one residue Jalisco has too much of.
impact: Inputs: pelletized agave bagasse from a local pelletizer, Pleurotus strains from the lab collection, low-cost sterile and fruiting equipment, and my cultivation protocol. Activities: pasteurize and inoculate substrate, grow and harvest, sell fresh mushrooms and kits, teach courses, in person and online, with and without the AI tutor, and breed strains for bagasse. Outputs in year one: one tonne (1,000 kilograms) of bagasse diverted from burning or dumping, at least 600 kilograms of gourmet mushrooms sold to Guadalajara restaurants through a distributor and to a 700-member gourmet community, the first strains screened for biological efficiency on bagasse, and at least two courses. Short-term outcomes: restaurants get fresh gourmet mushrooms grown a few kilometres away instead of produce brought from other states or imported, with less spoilage and a smaller transport footprint; and people who take a course leave able to grow mushrooms at home with a pressure cooker and a plastic tent. Medium-term outcome: a disposal cost for one distillery becomes a supply contract. Longer-term outcomes: a documented, open protocol and strain set that other growers in Latin America can apply to their own lignocellulosic residues, and less residue burned or dumped per tonne processed. Evidence so far: the 2026 PrepaTec pilot, on sawdust pellets, showed the system works outside a lab, with two harvests from one inoculation and 85 people reached; on unsupplemented agave bagasse pellets, triplicate bags reached about 50 percent biological efficiency in the first two weighed flushes; and grow-kit and course sales show willingness to pay. I will track kilograms of bagasse processed, kilograms harvested, biological efficiency per strain and substrate, revenue per channel, and people trained, disaggregated by sex, in a monthly production log.
techstack: Solid-state fermentation of lignocellulose by white-rot fungi, as Pleurotus does naturally: its enzymes degrade lignin and cellulose, and the fibre becomes fruiting bodies. Steps: hydration of pellets, pasteurization, inoculation with grain spawn produced on popcorn in a 39-litre pressure canner, incubation in bags, and fruiting in a negative-pressure room with filtered intake, an inline extractor and humidistat-controlled ultrasonic humidification. My own results: about 60 percent biological efficiency on sawdust pellets, and about 50 percent over two weighed flushes on unsupplemented agave bagasse pellets (triplicate, P. ostreatus var. columbinus); 20 percent soybean hull is the next step. Strain work uses classical genetics: Pleurotus ostreatus is tetrapolar, so crosses between sibling monokaryons are compatible only about 25 percent of the time; crossing two different parental strains in a factorial design escapes that limit, and compatibility is confirmed by clamp connections on confrontation plates. Biological efficiency is compared against the parental strains with one-way analysis of variance. Published work supports the approach: Pleurotus colonizes and fruits on agave bagasse (Larios-Ulloa and Ramírez-Muñoz, 2024; Arias García and Soto Velazco, 2025), with biological efficiencies of 41.2 to 65.7 percent (Lagunes-Reyes et al., 2023) and 56.7 percent for P. djamor on a bagasse and barley straw mix (Cruz-Moreno et al., 2023); the tetrapolar mating system is described by Eger (1978); monokaryon crosses of P. ostreatus have produced hybrids that outyield both parents (Rana et al., 2024); and yield in Pleurotus is heritable (Avin et al., 2016). The AI tutor is a ChatGPT-based assistant built with guidance and early support from Equitech Futures, delivered through Google Slides and tested against traditional teaching in a 50-student course; the next version will be a chatbot built on Claude. Everything is built so that a grower with a pressure cooker and a plastic tent can reproduce it.
business: The beneficiaries are distilleries that stop paying for disposal, restaurants and households in Guadalajara and nearby areas that get fresh local gourmet mushrooms, and growers who learn the method. Revenue comes from three lines. Fresh mushrooms, the main line at 600 kilograms in year one, sold to restaurants through a distributor (a restaurant supplier in my network reports producer prices of about 140 pesos per kilogram; a saleswoman who knows most of the city's restaurants has also offered to sell) and at a higher price directly to a 700-member gourmet food community. Grow kits sold to households and course participants, already selling with a positive margin. Courses, in person and later guided by the AI tutor; two paid courses for foreigners in 2026 brought in 6,000 pesos in a single day, half of it profit. The substrate costs about half of a conventional one, and each tonne of pellets should yield at least 600 kilograms of product, so unit economics work at small scale. Later lines are lion's mane, mini-kits with the AI tutor, and substrate processing for distilleries that want their bagasse handled on site.
